course.summary: Units, measurement and motion in a straight line: the foundations of mechanics.

skills.name: Use SI base units and derived units
Use v = u + at for uniform acceleration

sections.heading: Seven base units
sections.text: The SI system has seven base units, including the **metre** (length), **kilogram** (mass), **second** (time), **ampere** (current) and **kelvin** (temperature).

sections.heading: Derived units
sections.text: Other units are built from base units. Speed is m/s; force is the newton, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

sections.heading: Checking with units
sections.text: Both sides of a correct equation have the same units. Units in an answer are part of the answer.

questions.stem: Which is an SI base unit?
questions.explanation: The kilogram is a base unit; the others are derived.
hints: Base units can't be broken into other units.

questions.explanation: F = ma, so N = kg × m/s².

questions.stem: The SI unit of temperature is…
questions.explanation: The kelvin (K) is the SI base unit.

misconceptions.0: Celsius is common but not the SI base unit.

sections.heading: Why they matter
sections.text: Significant figures show how precise a measurement is. 2.50 m says more than 2.5 m: it is known to the nearest centimetre.

sections.heading: Counting rules
sections.text: All non-zero digits count. Zeros between them count (2.05 has 3). Leading zeros never count (0.0042 has 2). Trailing zeros after a decimal point count (3.400 has 4).

sections.heading: In calculations
sections.text: When multiplying or dividing, keep as many significant figures as the least precise number: 2.5 × 3.42 = 8.55 → 8.6.

questions.explanation: Leading zeros don't count; 3, 4 and the trailing 0 after the decimal do.
hints: Ignore zeros before the first non-zero digit.

misconceptions.0: The trailing zero after a decimal point counts.

questions.explanation: 3.0 has 2 significant figures, so the answer gets 2: 7.4.

misconceptions.0: Too many figures claim false precision.

boards.chapter: Chapter 2: Motion in a straight line

sections.heading: Distance vs displacement
sections.text: **Distance** is the total path length. **Displacement** is the straight-line change in position, with a direction. Walk 3 m east then 3 m west: distance 6 m, displacement 0.

sections.heading: Speed vs velocity
sections.text: Average speed = distance ÷ time. Average velocity = displacement ÷ time, and it has a direction.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: A car goes 60 km north in 1 h and returns in 1 h. Average speed = 120 km ÷ 2 h = 60 km/h; average velocity = 0.

questions.stem: A runner completes one full lap of a 400 m track. Displacement?
A cyclist rides 10 km east in 0.5 h. Average velocity?
Can average speed be zero while the object moved?
questions.explanation: If it moved, distance > 0, so average speed > 0. Average velocity can be zero.

misconceptions.0: That is true for velocity, not speed.

boards.chapter: Chapter 2: Motion in a straight line

sections.heading: Acceleration
sections.text: **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v − u) ÷ t, measured in m/s².

sections.heading: First equation of motion
sections.text: For uniform acceleration, **v = u + at**, where u is the initial velocity and v the velocity after time t.

sections.heading: Example
sections.text: A scooter starts at 2 m/s and accelerates at 1.5 m/s² for 4 s: v = 2 + 1.5 × 4 = 8 m/s.

questions.stem: A car goes from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s. Acceleration?
hints: a = (v − u) ÷ t; 'from rest' means u = 0.

questions.stem: u = 3 m/s, a = 2 m/s², t = 6 s. Find v.
A negative acceleration while moving forward means the object is…
questions.explanation: Acceleration opposite to velocity reduces speed.
hints: Compare the directions of a and v.

misconceptions.3: It still moves forward, just more slowly.
